Sole-authored survey by a condensed-matter physicist. It takes novelty (a property the parts lack) as the defining mark of emergence and sets it against twelve other characteristics in §2. The six "subjective" ones are self-organisation, unpredictability, irreducibility, contextuality/downward causation, complexity and intra-stratum closure. Case studies from the Ising model to Schelling segregation and LLMs show that each can come apart from novelty: novelty without discontinuity (Kondo, Fermi liquids, spin ice), without unpredictability (BKT, spin ice), and with reduction (Butterfield). §22 sides with weak emergence and argues that strong-emergence claims from molecular structure are weak. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 (NOTE-124); worth reading as a hub reference and example catalogue on emergence from physics outward, with unusually concrete case studies and a sceptical physicist's §15 on molecular structure. | [LIT-156](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-156.md) v4 | An Emerging Dilemma for Reciprocal Causation | Hazelwood (2023), DOI-10.1017/psa.2023.124. Hazelwood defines RC as "the process of natural selection is both a cause and effect of processes such as niche construction" and EC as "natural selection is an emergent causal process". He argues they are incompatible. Emergence here is Wilson's synchronic dependence plus autonomy, cashed out as Pence's composition. If EC holds, niche construction partly composes selection, so the two fail Woodward's independent-fixability condition and cannot stand in a causal relation. If EC fails, selection is either non-causal (statisticalism) or individual-level, which is incoherent because relative fitness needs a population (Millstein, Sober). EES proponents should drop RC but can keep niche construction as a genuine cause of the evolutionary *product*. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-137](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-137.md)); worth reading as a tight, well-sourced argument that brings the reciprocal-causation debate into the composition, exclusion and interventionism literature. | [LIT-157](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-157.md) v3 | Reproducees, reproducers, and Darwinian individuals | Bourrat (2025), DOI-10.1007/s11229-024-04880-w. Bourrat builds a nested vocabulary. A reproducee is a B that comes after A, is caused by A, and is of A's relevant class. A reproducer is a reproducee with reproductive autonomy, meaning it can reproduce across a range of backgrounds. A Darwinian individual is a reproducer with high reproductive causal control, meaning heredity survives as the parent's description is made finer. On that vocabulary, genes of multicellular organisms are, like hearts, mere reproducees, but with high control. Material overlap is necessary for reproducers, which are whole life cycles, and unnecessary for reproducees, so Griesemer and Godfrey-Smith partly talk past each other. Both quantities get an information-theoretic recipe (conditional MI after Bertschinger et al. 2008 for autonomy; interventional MI across grains, Griffiths et al.'s INF, for control), and neither is computed. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-100](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-100.md)); worth reading as the clearest statement of the reproduced/reproducing distinction and a tidy, well-scoped settlement of the material-overlap dispute. Its value is conceptual. Its two measures are recipes that are never computed, and the autonomy recipe does not match its own verbal definition. |

Lloyd's own four-question anatomy of "unit of selection": interactor, reproducer (formerly replicator), manifestor of adaptation, and beneficiary. She combines it with a split between two multilevel schools, Wrightian "Evolutionary Change" and Fisherian "Adaptationist/KS". She uses the two to argue for a verdict, not merely to map the debates. The verdict is that most rejections of group, species and holobiont selection come from demanding that an interactor also be a manifestor of *engineering* adaptation. | [LIT-169](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-169.md) v2 | Defining the niche for niche construction: evolutionary and ecological niches | Trappes (2021), DOI-10.1007/s10539-021-09805-2. Trappes compares NCT's evolutionary niche with the ecological niche. The evolutionary niche is the sum of selection pressures on a population (Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman 2003), read "externally" as the environmental factors that produce fitness differences. The ecological niche is the conditions that permit continued existence; for a population, mean absolute fitness ≥ 1. Even at their closest, against the realized population niche, the two differ in extension. Habitat degradation is in the evolutionary niche but not the ecological one, and commensalism and non-limiting resources are in the ecological niche but not the evolutionary one. He examines five standard arguments. Four fail: (a) Fisher's significance-test logic, (b) control of unknown confounders, (d) that observational studies "exaggerate" effects, and (e) probabilistic causality. The fifth, (c) selection bias, is a "cast-iron argument", but it supports only taking allocation out of the clinicians' hands, and randomisation is one way to do that. What matters is balance on plausible confounders, a placebo or active control and blinding. The paper sets out an idealized three-stage sequence of interaction types, which it calls a "first and rough sketch" (§1). Stage 1 is coordination in *collections* (pairwise, "aggregative" interactions of co-located individuals). Stage 2 is cooperation in *conexuses* (a connected web of binary interactions whose benefits can still be counted per member). Stage 3 is collaboration in *communities*: heterogeneous multi-way interactions around a shared goal, in which generatively entrenched "core" interactions give organizational closure. Table 1 puts the transition to a new level of individuality between stages 2 and 3 only. The paper asserts, rather than argues, that this describes evolutionary transitions non-circularly and that individuality is a special case of collectivity. Its one argued conclusion is hedged: community-level inheritance "seem[s] likely to evolve in tandem" with community-level individuality (§3). | Proposed — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-173](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-173.md)); a short programmatic sketch, and the authors call it one. Its headline claims (non-circularity; individuality as a special case of collectivity) appear only in the abstract. Two things would settle it: the model of community "reliability" and endogenization the authors promise in §2 ("We hope to explore such models in future work"), or an application of the 3Cs to a worked case, such as the companion Neolithic paper, that separates collection, conexus and community by measurable criteria. |

Bennett states Landauer's principle as a consequence of the Second Law. A logically irreversible step, meaning erasure or a *merge of control flow*, must export at least the lost entropy (k ln 2 per bit) to non-information-bearing degrees of freedom. That export need not take the form of heat (p. 1). Logically reversible operations, including copying onto a blank register and measurement, have no minimum cost. He calls "an intrinsic cost of order kT for every elementary act of information processing" a 20th-century "misconception" (pp. 5–6). A one-locus model in which an individual's genotype affects relatives' fitness. Weighting each effect by Wright's coefficient of relationship r gives "inclusive fitness", which tends to be maximized as classical fitness is. An action that costs the actor is favoured only if the benefit to a relative exceeds 1/r times the cost: more than two brothers, four half-brothers or eight first cousins (§5). It proves that mean inclusive fitness increases only for genes whose total effect on others is non-negative (giving traits); for harming traits it shows only that selection points uphill. It says nothing about morality: it is the kin domain of morality-as-cooperation in its biological form, read as biology. |

Applications range from cleaner fish to disease and nondisjunction. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-411](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-411.md)); worth reading as the formal statement of how reciprocity can start, spread and hold: tit-for-tat is robust in Axelrod's tournaments, cannot be bettered by any mutant when the continuation probability w is high enough, and can enter an all-defect population through kinship or clustering. It is not the source of the Hawk–Dove game or of owner–intruder conventions, though morality-as-cooperation cites it for both: its strategies are Mouse, Hawk, Bully, Retaliator and Prober-Retaliator, its contestants are symmetric, and its "Retaliator is an ESS" ties with Mouse, so it fails the paper's own second ESS condition. What it does ground for MAC's contest domains is restraint backed by retaliation, and, informally, retreat before a visibly superior opponent and honest signals of formidability. |
| [LIT-506](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-506.md) v2 | The Genetical Evolution of Social Behaviour. II | Hamilton (1964), J. Theor. Biol. 7:17–52. Part I's model is generalized, "unrigorously", into two principles: an animal values a neighbour's fitness against its own by their relationship, and its social discriminations evolve to make relationship more determinate. They are applied to alarm calls, clones and colonies, the haplodiploid hypothesis for hymenopteran sociality, multiple mating, fights between relatives, sibling competition and seed provisioning. Evidence is anecdotal, and the author reports where it runs against him. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-410](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-410.md)); worth reading as the place inclusive fitness is turned into two general principles (valuing neighbours by relatedness; evolving discrimination that makes relatedness determinate) and tried on warning behaviour, social insects, clones, fights and parental care. The principles are offered as an "unrigorous" generalization of Part I, and the evidence is anecdotal and, by the author's account, partly contrary. Its §6 on fights is the one place in Hamilton's pair that touches contests: relatives should fight less, a kin-weighted version of the restraint Maynard Smith and Price derived without kinship. |
| [LIT-508](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-508.md) | A mutualistic approach to morality: The evolution of fairness by partner choice | Baumard, André & Sperber (2013), DOI-10.1017/S0140525X11002202. When individuals can choose partners and have equal outside options, a split that gives one side less than it could get elsewhere is not stable, so partner choice selects for sharing the gains of cooperation in proportion to contribution. Competition to be chosen then favours a genuine, non-instrumental sense of fairness. Economic-game results (entitlement effects, merit-based division, need-based mutual aid, proportionate punishment) are reinterpreted as fairness, not altruism. Morality is defined as fairness; kin care and group loyalty are not intrinsically moral. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-407](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-407.md)), with all 28 open peer commentaries and the authors' Response; worth reading as the strongest single-mechanism cooperative theory of morality and as the parent of moral disciplining ([LIT-101](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-101.md)). It is a cooperation theory that cuts the other way from morality-as-cooperation: partner choice selects one moral sense, fairness, and kin care and group loyalty are not intrinsically moral. Its evidence is a reinterpretation of others' economic-game results, and its central formal claim is cited from the authors' separate model. The commentaries (Graham, Ramlakhan & Brook, Machery & Stich, Sachdeva et al., Atran) press the purity, harm and scope objections, and the Response answers them two ways because the authors disagree among themselves. |
| [LIT-510](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-510.md) | The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism | Trivers (1971), DOI-10.1086/406755. Altruism between non-relatives can be selected if acts cost the giver less than they benefit the recipient, the same partners meet repeatedly and symmetrically, and altruists stop helping those who fail to reciprocate. Cleaner-fish hosts fit; bird alarm calls are explained instead by self-interest. In humans, friendship, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, guilt, suspicion and their sham versions are proposed as adaptations that regulate exchange, and rules of conduct as a multiparty extension. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-402](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-402.md)); worth reading as the source of reciprocal altruism and, for this record above all, of the first adaptive account of moral emotions: moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, guilt and the detection of sham versions of each, with "norms of reciprocal conduct" as a later step. The formal part is slight (a verbal model and Hamilton's communicated Prisoner's Dilemma sketch); the human psychology is hypothesis supported by the social-psychology literature of the 1960s. It grounds the exchange domain of morality-as-cooperation and gives that domain its emotions. |
| [LIT-514](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-514.md) v3 | Moral Origins: The Evolution of Virtue, Altruism, and Shame | Boehm (2012), Basic Books. By the publisher's account, the moral sense is "a sophisticated defense mechanism": group punishment of bullies, thieves, free riders and psychopaths over six million years made social selection favour altruists and bred conscience, virtue and shame. The chapter list adds a "selection-by-reputation hypothesis" and its test. Unread: filed from the description and chapter list. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The book is lending-only at the Internet Archive (item moraloriginsevol0000boeh) and sold by Basic Books. What it argues is known here only from the publisher's description, labelled as such. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-515](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-515.md) | Statistical physics of self-replication | England (2012; J. Chem. Phys. 2013), arXiv:1209.1179. For a system in a heat bath obeying detailed balance, a transition between coarse-grained ensembles I → II obeys β⟨ΔQ⟩ + ln π(II→I) + ΔS_int ≥ 0 (Eq. 6), a second law stated for macrostates. Applied to self-replication, the reverse probability is small when the copy is durable and made fast, so the heat released per copy is bounded below by about 2n ln(n τ_decay/τ_div) − ΔS_int (Eq. 8). The author's estimates put E. coli within a factor of three of this bound and a self-replicating RNA near it. The "self" in self-replication is an observer's classification of microstates, not a physical given. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-419](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-419.md)), from arXiv v1, the only arXiv version; the published J. Chem. Phys. text was not reached. Worth reading as the founding paper of the "dissipation-driven" programme and as a clean worked use of a macrostate fluctuation relation: the heat a replicator must release is bounded below by how fast it copies and how durable the copy is, not by the copying itself. The general bound (Eq. 6) is a coarse-grained second law and is sound; the numbers for E. coli and RNA rest on an argued, not derived, upper bound on the reverse probability (Eq. 7). It draws no line between living and non-living replicators, and says so: "self" is a classification an observer supplies. |
| [LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md) | Time, Structure and Fluctuations | Prigogine (1977), Nobel Lecture, reprinted in Science 201:777 (1978). Near equilibrium the second-order excess entropy δ²S is a Lyapounov function, so fluctuations die out, and in the "strictly" linear regime the steady state minimizes entropy production. Far from equilibrium the sign of the excess entropy production ΣδJδX is no longer fixed. Given autocatalytic steps (necessary, not sufficient) the thermodynamic branch can go unstable, and fluctuations are amplified into "dissipative structures": Bénard convection, the Brusselator's limit cycle and "Turing bifurcation". A closing programme derives irreversibility from a non-unitary transformation of the Liouville dynamics. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-424](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-424.md)); worth reading as Prigogine's own short statement of the dissipative-structure programme, and as the place where its scope limits are stated in his words. A dissipative structure is a state beyond an instability of the "thermodynamic branch", "a giant fluctuation stabilized by exchanges of energy with the outside world". The minimum-entropy-production theorem is valid only in the "strictly" linear regime with constant phenomenological coefficients. Far from equilibrium the only general criterion offered is a sufficient one for stability (non-negative excess entropy production). Its §§6–7 programme of a non-unitary "entropy operator" is a sketch whose demonstrated link to macroscopic thermodynamics is, by its own account, "at least in the linear region". |
| [LIT-517](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-517.md) | Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences | Jarzynski (1997), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690. For a classical system that starts in canonical equilibrium and is switched from Hamiltonian H_0 to H_1 at any finite rate, the average of e^{−βW} over repetitions equals e^{−βΔF} (Eq. 2), whatever the path and the switching time. The proof is exact for an isolated system and for Nosé–Hoover thermostats, and needs weak coupling for a physical reservoir. Thermodynamic integration and the Zwanzig perturbation formula are its slow and fast limits, and ⟨W⟩ ≥ ΔF follows by Jensen. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-417](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-417.md)); worth reading as the four-page origin of the nonequilibrium work relation ⟨e^{−βW}⟩ = e^{−βΔF}: an equality, independent of path and switching rate, that turns irreversible work measurements into an equilibrium free-energy difference and gives ⟨W⟩ ≥ ΔF as a corollary by Jensen. Read it knowing two things. The physical-reservoir proof rests on weak coupling (Eq. 9 → 10), which the author states; and its usefulness is limited by the author's own estimate to work fluctuations of order k_BT, so nanoscale systems or simulations. |
| [LIT-518](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-518.md) | Statistical Physics of Adaptation | Perunov, Marsland & England (2014; Phys. Rev. X 2016), arXiv:1412.1875. Starting from a fluctuation relation between coarse-grained macrostates, the paper writes the log-odds of two outcomes of a driven system as an internal-entropy term, a reversal-probability term and Ψ − Φ, the mean heat minus a fluctuation correction (Eq. 8). Holding the first two fixed, the more likely outcome is the one whose formation absorbed and dissipated work from the drive more reliably. It calls such outcomes "adapted" and argues the tendency needs no self-replication. Two single-particle hopping models illustrate the dissipation and fluctuation terms (Eqs. 10–13); the many-body case is a plausibility argument. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-416](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-416.md)), from arXiv v1, the only arXiv version; the published Physical Review X text was not reached. Worth reading as the origin of "dissipative adaptation": the claim that driven matter tends towards states whose formation absorbed and dissipated work reliably, with no replication needed. Read it as a heuristic argument with two toy models, not a theorem. Its exact content is a rearranged macrostate fluctuation relation; the step to "adaptation" holds two terms fixed that it does not show can be held fixed in a many-body system, and the simulation it reports was not shown. It deliberately erases the line between living and non-living organization. |
| [LIT-519](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-519.md) | Nonequilibrium thermodynamics and maximum entropy production in the Earth system | Kleidon (2009), DOI-10.1007/s00114-009-0509-x. A review of MEP in the Earth system. MEP is the proposed principle that a system with enough degrees of freedom adopts the steady state of maximum entropy production. It selects among steady states, where Prigogine's principle only describes relaxation toward one. Box models show the flux–force trade-off that gives an MEP state. The review estimates the Earth's entropy budget, which is dominated by absorption of sunlight. It surveys MEP fits for atmosphere, ocean, mantle, hydrology and biota, and proposes that life drives the planet toward MEP, a thermodynamic reading of Gaia. The author grants that MEP is not established. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-423](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-423.md)); worth reading as the clearest statement of the maximum-entropy-production (MEP) programme in Earth-system science by its main advocate: what MEP claims, how it differs from Prigogine's minimum principle (minimum entropy production describes relaxation toward a steady state; MEP selects among possible steady states), an order-of-magnitude entropy budget of the Earth, a survey of climate, ocean, mantle and biotic MEP applications, and the extension to life and Gaia. Read it as advocacy that is candid about its footing: the author calls MEP "proposed" and says "no one would argue that MEP is well established". Chosen over the Kleidon–Lorenz 2005 book, which has no lawful open text. |
| [LIT-520](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-520.md) v2 | Maximum entropy production principle in physics, chemistry and biology | Martyushev & Seleznev (2006), DOI-10.1016/j.physrep.2005.12.001. A 45-page Physics Reports review of the maximum entropy production principle (MEPP) across physics, chemistry and biology. Kleidon (2009) cites it as the review of MEP's physical foundation. Semantic Scholar's machine-generated summary says it analyses the principle's thermodynamic and statistical basis, including its relation to the second law and to Prigogine's principle. Unread: no text or abstract reached. | Unavailable — seeded 2026-10-02 from Crossref metadata and citing works, not read: no lawful full text or publisher abstract could be reached (Physics Reports, closed; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex list no open copy, and the abstract is elided by the publisher). Filed because it is the main survey of the maximum-entropy-production principle and of its relation to Prigogine's minimum principle; it stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-521](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-521.md) | Information theory explanation of the fluctuation theorem, maximum entropy production and self-organized criticality in non-equilibrium stationary states | Dewar (2003), DOI-10.1088/0305-4470/36/3/303. It applies Jaynes's maximum-entropy inference to the microscopic paths of an open system in a stationary state. Under fixed initial densities and boundary fluxes plus local conservation, the path distribution is p_Γ ∝ exp(A_Γ), with A_Γ carrying τσ_Γ/2k_B (Eq. 14). A fluctuation theorem and ⟨σ⟩ ≥ 0 follow (Eqs. 18–21). Then, in a mean-field approximation and assuming the number of paths increases with irreversible action, maximizing path entropy over the remaining multipliers is maximizing mean entropy production (MaxEP, Eq. 24). A Landau–Ginzburg argument claims self-organized criticality as slow driving goes to zero. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-426](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-426.md)); worth reading as the founding attempt to derive the maximum-entropy-production principle (MaxEP) from Jaynes's maximum-entropy inference over microscopic paths, and as the source most later MEP work, Kleidon's included, cites for MEP's theoretical foundation. Read it as a programme, not a proof. The path distribution p_Γ ∝ exp(A_Γ) and its fluctuation theorem follow from the stated constraints. The MaxEP step needs a mean-field approximation and an assumption that the number of paths grows with their irreversible action, which is stated, not argued. The self-organized-criticality corollary is a mean-field artefact by Grinstein and Linsker's analysis ([LIT-525](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-525.md)), which this reading confirms. |
| [LIT-522](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-522.md) | Entropy production fluctuation theorem and the nonequilibrium work relation for free energy differences | Crooks (1999), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevE.60.2721. For finite classical systems with stochastic, Markovian, microscopically reversible dynamics, the entropy production ω of a forward process and of its time reverse satisfy P_F(+ω)/P_R(−ω) = e^{ω} for any finite time, provided ω is odd under reversal. That holds for processes that start and end in equilibrium, where ω = β(W − ΔF), and for time-symmetric nonequilibrium steady states. The Jarzynski equality follows in one line, and for long times the theorem gives a heat fluctuation theorem and a Gaussian with variance twice the mean. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-413](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-413.md)); worth reading as the short paper that turned the entropy-production fluctuation theorem into a finite-time, trajectory-level statement for stochastic, microscopically reversible dynamics, P_F(+ω)/P_R(−ω) = e^{ω}, and derived the Jarzynski equality from it in a line. It also defines the trajectory entropy production ω = ln ρ(x_{−τ}) − ln ρ(x_{+τ}) − βQ that the record's stochastic-thermodynamics papers inherit. Read it knowing that its conditions are stated exactly (finite classical system, constant-intensive-parameter baths, Markovian microscopically reversible dynamics, ω odd under time reversal), and that the steady-state version is formally exact but, by the author's own account, of little practical use. |
| [LIT-523](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-523.md) | Stochastic thermodynamics, fluctuation theorems and molecular machines | Seifert (2012), DOI-10.1088/0034-4885/75/12/126001. A 105-page review of stochastic thermodynamics. Work, heat and a stochastic system entropy s = −ln p(x(τ),τ) are defined along single trajectories of Markovian systems coupled to baths, and every known integral, detailed and Crooks fluctuation theorem is derived from one master theorem by choosing a conjugate dynamics. Further results: dissipation bounds forward–reverse distinguishability (⟨w⟩ − ΔF ≥ D[p‖p_eq]), Sagawa–Ueda feedback relations, a NESS fluctuation–dissipation theorem in terms of entropy production, and a cycle-based theory of efficiency at maximum power for molecular machines. | Active — read 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-420](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-420.md); §§5, 8.3–8.4, 9.2 and 11 skimmed); worth reading as the systematic reference for stochastic thermodynamics as of 2012: first law, heat and stochastic entropy along single trajectories of Markovian systems coupled to baths, every known fluctuation theorem derived from one master theorem with a conjugate dynamics, dissipation as distinguishability of forward and reverse paths, Sagawa–Ueda feedback, the NESS fluctuation–dissipation theorem and efficiency of molecular machines. It is the framework in which the record's thermodynamics-of-prediction and thermodynamics-of-learning results ([LIT-327](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-327.md), [LIT-308](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-308.md)) are stated. Read it as a review: the derivations are its own and concise, the case studies are reported. |
| [LIT-524](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-524.md) v2 | Self-Organization in Nonequilibrium Systems: From Dissipative Structures to Order through Fluctuations | Nicolis & Prigogine (1977), Wiley-Interscience. The Brussels school's monograph on self-organization far from equilibrium, from the thermodynamics and bifurcation theory of dissipative structures to their stochastic theory ("order through fluctuations"). The Nobel lecture cites its ch. VII for the Brusselator and the book for its catalogue of chemical and biological examples. Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scan is a lending-only copy, HathiTrust is search-only, and no publisher description or table of contents was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the Brussels school's book-length treatment of dissipative structures and "order through fluctuations", and the source the Nobel lecture ([LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md)) gives for the Brusselator; what it contains beyond that is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-525](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-525.md) | Comments on a derivation and application of the ‘maximum entropy production’ principle | Grinstein & Linsker (2007), DOI-10.1088/1751-8113/40/31/N01. A Comment with two points. (1) Dewar's 2005 derivation of MaxEP needs a quadratic approximation to p(f) near f = F to hold for all f. With the fluctuation theorem, that forces A(F) to be constant, i.e. linear constitutive relations. So the "orthogonality condition" behind both maximum and minimum entropy production fails far from equilibrium, as an exact spin-chain model shows. (2) Dewar's 2003 SOC result is an artefact. Keeping the quartic term gives a finite flux variance at F_ext = 0. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-422](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-422.md)); worth reading as the short, exact critique of Dewar's information-theoretic derivation of maximum entropy production. It shows that the 2005 derivation's key step holds only where the constitutive relations are linear, so MaxEP far from equilibrium is not established by it, and that the 2003 claim that MaxEP yields self-organized criticality is an artefact of a mean-field expansion. Read from the authors' submitted manuscript (Zenodo); the version of record was not seen. Its first point is checked here only on its own worked example, since Dewar 2005 itself could not be read. |
| [LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md) | Life as we know it | Friston (2013), J. R. Soc. Interface 10(86):20130475. Any ergodic random dynamical system whose states split into internal, sensory, active and external sets with a Markov blanket has internal and active states whose flow can be written as a gradient descent on a variational free energy of the blanket and internal states (Lemma 2.1, Eqs. 2.5–2.8). They therefore "appear" to do Bayesian inference about external states and to bound their own entropy. A simulated "primordial soup" of 128 coupled Lorenz subsystems forms a blanket-enclosed cluster whose internal states predict external motion (5 of 82 above a time-reversed null) and which disperses when blanket or internal states are lesioned. The paper says a candle flame cannot have a Markov blanket, and concedes that the universe holds countless blankets, conjecturing that minimum-entropy blankets mark life. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-421](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-421.md)), from the published text (the author's posted PDF of the journal version and the PMC full text). Worth reading as the founding statement of the Markov-blanket formulation of the free energy principle applied to life, and as the one text in the record that names a candle flame and says it is not lifelike. Read it as a redescription, not a derivation: its "heuristic proof" shows that the flow of an ergodic system with a Markov blanket can be written as a gradient flow on a variational free energy, by choosing the variational density to equal the posterior. The free energy is variational, not thermodynamic; no heat or entropy production is computed. The simulation is one run, analysed with a blanket chosen by spectral clustering. |
| [LIT-527](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-527.md) | Pattern formation outside of equilibrium | Cross & Hohenberg (1993), DOI-10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851. A 262-page review classifying non-equilibrium patterns by the linear instability of a uniform state: type I_s (finite wave-number, stationary: convection rolls, Turing patterns), III_o (uniform oscillation: the stirred BZ reaction) and I_o (travelling waves). Near threshold, universal amplitude equations describe them, and phase equations describe them further above it. It finds no general variational principle for non-equilibrium steady states, only perturbative ones near threshold. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-418](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-418.md)), about 30 of 262 pages read closely; worth reading as the physicists' standard account of pattern formation away from equilibrium, and as the sober counterweight to the dissipative-structure programme. It treats Rayleigh–Bénard convection, Turing patterns and the BZ reaction in one framework, classifying patterns by the linear instability of a uniform state and describing them near onset by universal amplitude equations. Its conclusion finds "no evidence for the existence of any global minimization principles controlling the structure, except as a perturbative statement near threshold", and quotes Glansdorff and Prigogine conceding as much. |
| [LIT-528](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-528.md) | Energy flow and the organization of life | Morowitz & Smith (2006 working paper; Complexity 2007). Life may be forced into existence by abiotic free-energy sources, as lightning and hurricanes are channels that relieve electric and thermal potentials. Core anabolism, the reductive citric-acid cycle and the cascade built on it, is read as a relaxation channel for geochemical redox and phosphate energy. Jaynes-style entropy maximization with current-dependent entropies (not entropy-production principles) is offered as the framework, and the emergence of life as a "collapse", a phase transition of a metastable abiotic earth. Selection on metabolism comes before replication. No quantitative model is given; the authors say the claim is undemonstrated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-425](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-425.md)), from the Santa Fe Institute working paper (2006-08-029, dated 7 August 2006), not the Complexity version of record. Filed in place of Morowitz's 1968 book Energy Flow in Biology, which could not be read: every Internet Archive scan of it is lending-only. Worth reading as a short statement of the "life was inevitable" view by Morowitz and Smith: core metabolism, the reductive citric-acid cycle, is a channel geochemistry was forced to open to relieve free-energy stresses, as lightning relieves a charge separation. It is an essay. It says itself that the claim "has not been quantitatively demonstrated", and its evidence is the structure of core metabolism read in that light. It puts life on a continuum with lightning and hurricanes and draws no principled line. |
| [LIT-530](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-530.md) v2 | What Is Life? The Physical Aspect of the Living Cell | Schrödinger (1944), Cambridge University Press. Lectures given at Trinity College Dublin in February 1943, published as a short book for the lay reader. It asks how events inside a living organism can be accounted for by physics and chemistry. It treats the gene as an "aperiodic crystal" carrying a code-script, defended through the Delbrück model, and in chapter 6 says an organism keeps its order by drawing "order from order" and by feeding on negative entropy from its surroundings. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and contents; the text itself was not reached. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, the Cambridge Core contents and chapter excerpts, and library catalogue records, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The book is in copyright with Cambridge University Press. Every Internet Archive scan of a Cambridge or Macmillan printing is lending-only, and the freely downloadable PDFs that turn up (course sites, personal uploads, Internet Archive "opensource" uploads) are unauthorized copies of the Canto edition, so I did not open them. Chapter 6, the negative-entropy chapter, is unread beyond the publisher's one-paragraph excerpt. |
| [LIT-531](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-531.md) | Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction | Zhabotinsky (2007), Scholarpedia 2(9):1435. BZ reactions are metal-ion-catalysed oxidations of organic reductants by bromate in acid. The core loop is autocatalytic oxidation of the catalyst via HBrO₂, switched off by bromide, which the oxidized catalyst regenerates from bromomalonic acid. Closed, stirred, it can run "up to several thousand" cycles; only in a continuous-flow reactor do oscillations continue indefinitely, and there bursting and chaos appear. Unstirred thin layers support target and spiral waves (Zaikin & Zhabotinsky 1970). The Oregonator is qualitatively right and quantitatively not. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-414](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-414.md)); worth reading as the short, authoritative account of the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction by the chemist who named half of it: discovery, the core mechanism (autocatalytic HBrO₂ inhibited by Br⁻), the Oregonator and its known defects, closed versus open-reactor dynamics, and target and spiral waves. Chosen over Zaikin & Zhabotinsky (1970) because it is openly readable and covers the 1970 waves paper; it is a short encyclopedia review with no new results. |
| [LIT-532](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-532.md) v2 | Inadequacy of entropy and entropy derivatives in characterizing the steady state | Landauer (1975), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevA.12.636. Per its abstract: in a bistable system the kinetics of transitions between the two locally stable states can be changed without changing the behaviour near either state, so no quantity that characterises only the vicinity of the states can determine which is more probable. Separately, even a monostable linear circuit's steady state need not be one of minimum entropy production. Unread: filed from the abstract. | Unavailable — seeded 2026-10-02 from its abstract and Crossref metadata, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (Physical Review A, closed; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex list no open copy). Filed because it is the classic objection to entropy-based characterisations of nonequilibrium steady states, Prigogine's minimum principle among them; it stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-533](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-533.md) | Life as a manifestation of the second law of thermodynamics | Schneider & Kay (1994), Math. Comput. Modelling 19(6–8):25–48. A "restated second law": systems moved from equilibrium "utilize all avenues available to counter the applied gradients". Bénard convection and a vortex draining a bottle are read as structures that destroy gradients faster. Life is "another means of dissipating the solar induced gradient" (living systems as "sophisticated mini-tornados, with a memory"), and ecosystems develop to degrade more incoming exergy. A stressed marsh shows smaller flows and fewer cycles; airborne thermal scans show mature forests cooler (degrading 90% of net solar radiation against a quarry's 62%). The second law is "necessary but not sufficient" for life. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-415](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-415.md)), from the authors' own formatted text (copyright line "James J. Kay and Eric Schneider, 1992"), not the journal's typeset version. Worth reading as the canonical statement of the "gradient-dissipation" view of life: living systems and ecosystems are dissipative structures that develop so as to degrade the solar gradient more completely, and the second law is "a necessary but not sufficient cause for life". Read the thermodynamics as a programme, not a derivation. The "restated second law" is offered as a corollary of Kestin's stability result but not derived from it. The ecological evidence is one stressed-versus-control marsh pair and a few thermal-scanner and satellite comparisons, all correlational. It draws no line between living and non-living dissipative structures beyond "memory" (DNA). |
| [LIT-534](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-534.md) v2 | Order Out of Chaos: Man's New Dialogue with Nature | Prigogine & Stengers (1984), Bantam; based on their La nouvelle alliance. A book for general readers that sets the science of complexity and irreversibility against classical dynamics. By its contents: the rise and limits of Newtonian science and its philosophical reception (Diderot, Kant, Hegel, Bergson, Whitehead); thermodynamics from Carnot to Boltzmann's order principle; linear and far-from-equilibrium thermodynamics, bifurcations and order through fluctuations; and the rediscovery of time in physics. Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records and a partial contents note; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scans of the Bantam and Flamingo printings are lending-only, HathiTrust is search-only), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the popular and philosophical statement of the programme whose technical core is the Nobel lecture ([LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md)); what it argues, beyond its contents, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-535](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-535.md) | The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis | Turing (1952), DOI-10.1098/rstb.1952.0012. Chemicals ("morphogens") that react and diffuse through tissue can turn a stable homogeneous state unstable, with random disturbances setting which pattern grows. On a ring of cells the linearized onset takes six forms. The most important is stationary waves of finite "chemical wave-length", which (9.4a, b) allow for two morphogens only if they diffuse at different rates. A 20-cell example computed on the Manchester computer gives a three-lobed pattern. Hydra tentacles, whorled leaves, dappling and gastrulation are suggested applications, not tested ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-427](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-427.md)); worth reading as the founding paper of reaction–diffusion pattern formation and the origin of what the Brussels school later called the "Turing bifurcation". A homogeneous, stable steady state of reacting and diffusing chemicals can be destabilized by diffusion itself and settle into a stationary pattern with an intrinsic "chemical wave-length". The analysis is linear and near onset by design, every biological application is offered as suggestion, and the paper says outright that its patterns are "dynamic equilibria" fed by "a continual supply of free energy", which places them among dissipative structures before the term existed. |
| [LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md) v4 | Biological Autonomy: A Philosophical and Theoretical Enquiry | Moreno & Mossio (2015), Springer, History, Philosophy and Theory of the Life Sciences 12. The book argues that biology should revolve around autonomy, not only natural selection: organisms are organized systems that self-produce and self-maintain as integrated wholes, set their own goals and norms, and promote the conditions of their existence through interaction with their environment. Chapters treat constraints and organisational closure, emergence and inter-level causation, teleology and function, agency, evolution, organisms and levels of autonomy, and cognition. Only the Introduction is read ([NOTE-1437](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1437.md)): there the authors make closure of constraints the core of biological organisation, say it differs fundamentally from the self-organisation of dissipative structures, and announce that it grounds teleology, normativity and function; the chapters that argue this are unread. | Unfetched — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list. The book is not open access at Springer. Its only free copy, the authors' HAL deposit (hal-01151449, hal.science/hal-01151449/document, CC BY-NC 4.0, deposited 13 May 2015), is not the whole book, as this note earlier said: it holds the front matter (Hooker's Foreword and the contents), the Introduction (pp. xix–xxxiv), the references and the index, and no chapter. The Introduction was read in full on 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1437](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1437.md), Skimmed, because only the Introduction was read). For chapters 1–8 no fuller lawful copy was found: on 2026-10-30 OpenAlex listed the HAL deposit as the book's only open copy, and the publisher's chapters are paywalled. HAL also served its anti-bot page to a direct fetch on 2026-10-02 and again on 2026-10-30; the deposit was read from a copy retrieved earlier the same day. It stays Unfetched for the chapters. |

The monograph of the Brussels thermodynamic stability theory. By the Nobel lecture's citations, it treats local equilibrium (ch. II), the second-order excess entropy δ²S as a Lyapounov function near equilibrium (ch. V), and the excess-entropy-production criterion far from equilibrium, including convection (ch. VII). Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scan is a lending-only copy, HathiTrust is search-only, and no publisher description or table of contents was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. The paper that named the biopsychosocial model. | [LIT-566](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-566.md) | Defining Agency: Individuality, Normativity, Asymmetry, and Spatio-temporality in Action | Barandiaran, Di Paolo & Rohde (2009), Adaptive Behavior 17(5):367–386. Three conditions are jointly necessary and sufficient for minimal agency: the system defines its own individuality, it is the active source of modulations of its coupling with the environment (interactional asymmetry), and it regulates that coupling by norms it generates (normativity). Generatively, an agent is an open autonomous system (a precarious network of mutually enabling processes) that adaptively modulates its coupling so as to maintain some of its constituent processes. Minimal life satisfies this; life is sufficient for agency but not necessary. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-458](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-458.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the standard organizational definition of minimal agency, and as the clearest statement that an agent is not the same thing as an individual. Individuality is one of three conditions, with interactional asymmetry and normativity; it is a precondition for the other two and is not sufficient for agency. The generative definition: an agent is an autonomous organization that adaptively regulates its coupling with its environment and contributes to sustaining itself as a consequence. The paper rejects statistical and energetic measures of asymmetry as sufficient, and says systems optimising an externally fixed function should not be treated as models of agency. |
| [LIT-570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-570.md) | An Organizational Account of Biological Functions | Mossio, Saborido & Moreno (2009), BJPS 60(4):813–841. A trait has a function iff it contributes to the maintenance of a self-maintaining organization, is produced and maintained under that organization's constraints, and the organization is differentiated. Closure grounds teleology and normativity in the current system, unifying etiological and dispositional accounts. Flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes have closure but no functions, because each makes a single undifferentiated contribution to its own maintenance. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-444](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-444.md)), from the HAL deposit of the submitted version. Worth reading as the organizational account of function and as the place where the organizational school says plainly that a candle flame has closure. Functions are contributions to a differentiated self-maintaining organization by traits that organization produces and maintains. Closure alone grounds teleology and norms but is shared by flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes; organizational differentiation is what functions need. Reproduction is admitted to be a problem and left to a sketch. |
| [LIT-582](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-582.md) | Biological organisation as closure of constraints | Montévil & Mossio (2015), J. Theor. Biol. 372:179–191. Two causal regimes act in organisms: processes (thermodynamic changes) and constraints, which act on processes while being conserved at the relevant time scale. Closure is mutual dependence among constraints: each is produced by a process another constraint constrains, and each helps produce another. Closure mixes slow and fast dependence, grounds functions, and is proposed as a boundary criterion. A volume-sweeping count of dependencies, the tendency to closure, separates symbionts that share an encompassing closure, and separated nested closures mark levels of organisation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-468](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-468.md)), from the authors' HAL deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the paper statement of the central claim of Biological Autonomy ([LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md)): biological organisation is closure of constraints. A constraint is defined by a symmetry: it acts on a process at a time scale at which it is itself conserved. Closure is a set of constraints each of which depends directly on another in the set and generates another, and cannot be split into two closed sets. The paper offers closure as a boundary criterion and gives a preliminary measure, the tendency to closure, for drawing boundaries between interacting organisms. It does not claim closure defines an organism. |
| [LIT-588](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-588.md) v3 | A theoretical model of phase transitions in human hand movements | Haken, Kelso & Bunz (1985), Biological Cybernetics 51(5):347–356. Models the involuntary switch from anti-phase to in-phase finger or hand movement as movement frequency rises: relative phase φ is the order parameter, φ̇ = −∂V/∂φ with V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ, both patterns are stable while \|b\| > \|a\|/4 and only in-phase below it, and hysteresis follows. The φ equation is derived from two self-sustained oscillators whose coupling must be nonlinear, with amplitude falling as frequency rises acting as the control. A theory paper: its data are Kelso's earlier experiments, summarized. | Active — read 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1424](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1424.md)) in full, from the publisher's scan posted on Kelso's lab page at Florida Atlantic University (https://ccs.fau.edu/hbblab/pdfs/1985_Haken_Kelso_Bunz_Biol_Cyb.pdf); worth reading as the paper that states the HKB model: relative phase as order parameter, the potential V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ with anti-phase lost when b/a falls below 1/4, and its derivation from two nonlinearly coupled limit-cycle oscillators. Read it knowing that it is a theory paper with one numerical simulation and no new data: the switch and the hysteresis it models are summarized from Kelso's earlier experiments, and critical fluctuations and critical slowing are named as future work, not reported. |
| [LIT-601](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-601.md) | The Haken–Kelso–Bunz (HKB) model: from matter to movement to mind | Kelso (2021), Biological Cybernetics 115(4):305–322, a 60th-anniversary retrospective. HKB models bimanual coordination by the relative phase φ, with dφ/dt = −a sin φ − 2b sin 2φ and potential V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ: both in-phase and anti-phase are stable for b/a > 1/4, and anti-phase loses stability below it, as observed when movement frequency rises. Noise, symmetry breaking (Δω) and metastability extend it; with Kuramoto's model it becomes a generalized HKB for many agents. The same dynamics is reported within a body, between people and with machines, and in brain activity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-467](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-467.md)), from the free-to-read publisher PDF. Filed in place of Kelso's book Dynamic Patterns ([LIT-578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-578.md)) and as the read account of the paywalled Haken–Kelso–Bunz paper ([LIT-588](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-588.md)), both Deferred. Worth reading as Kelso's own short statement of coordination dynamics: the HKB order-parameter equation for relative phase, its stochastic and symmetry-breaking extensions, metastability as relative coordination, the generalized HKB–Kuramoto model, and the claim that one coordination dynamics holds within and between people. It is a retrospective by an author of the model, not a review, and it says so. |
| [LIT-627](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-627.md) v2 | At the crossroad of the search for spontaneous radiation and the Orch OR consciousness theory | Derakhshani, Diósi, Laubenstein, Piscicchia & Curceanu (2022), Physics of Life Reviews 42:8–14. By its abstract: a critical analysis of Orch OR against new bounds on the spontaneous radiation that the simplest gravity-related dynamical collapse model predicts, concluding that Orch OR built on that simplest version is "highly implausible in all the cases analyzed". Unread: registered from the abstract and the reference list. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-03 from the abstract, keywords and reference list, not read. The article is closed access at Elsevier. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Europe PMC list no open copy; there is no arXiv version (searched by title, abstract phrase and author pairs); Diósi's publication list gives the DOI but, unlike his other 2022 papers, no PDF; ScienceDirect returned a bot challenge and CORE a redirect challenge, so I stopped. A human reader with library access, or a copy requested from the authors, would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-628](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-628.md) | Homeostatic feelings and the biology of consciousness | Damasio & Damasio (2022), Brain 145(7):2231–2235, an Essay. Consciousness occurs when mind contents are spontaneously identified as belonging to their organism, and a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings (hunger, pain, well-being, plain feelings of existence) supplies that identification and "lends" consciousness to exteroceptive images. Feelings are hybrid: interoceptive pathways are unmyelinated, partly non-synaptic and unprotected by a blood–brain barrier, so the body and its neural map interact directly. Posterior brainstem lesions abolish consciousness where large cortical ones may not; consciousness needs "a partnership of nervous systems with the bodies they serve". | Active — skimmed 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-507](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-507.md)): every section was covered, but through a fetch tool that returned section-by-section accounts with short quotes, not a verbatim copy, so the quotes are unchecked; worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the Damasios' claim that consciousness is the spontaneous identification of mind contents as one's own, supplied by a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings, which are hybrid: in interoception the map and the body it maps interact and "commingle". It is a five-page Essay with no data. Its evidence is clinical and cited (brainstem coma versus cortical lesions, general anaesthesia), and its mechanism is the cellular contrast in Table 1: unmyelinated, non-synaptic, barrier-free interoceptive pathways. |
| [LIT-645](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-645.md) | Ultraviolet Superradiance from Mega-Networks of Tryptophan in Biological Architectures | Babcock et al. (2024), J. Phys. Chem. B 128(17):4035–4046, [ARXIV-2302.01469](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01469). Modelling tryptophan 1La transition dipoles in tubulin architectures with a radiative non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in the single-excitation limit, the authors predict strongly superradiant states (up to about 4000 times the single-tryptophan rate in a centriole, about 7000 extrapolated for large axon-like bundles) and a thermal quantum yield that rises with network size and survives static disorder of room-temperature size. Steady-state spectroscopy of taxol-stabilised porcine microtubules in buffer gives a tryptophan quantum yield of 17.6 ± 2.1% against 10.6 ± 0.6% for tubulin dimers, which they read as superradiance. Lifetimes, and so radiative rates, were not measured. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-509](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-509.md)); worth reading as the measured, room-temperature part of the case for collective quantum optical states in microtubules: a radiative-Hamiltonian model of up to more than 10⁵ tryptophan transition dipoles in microtubules, centrioles and axon-like bundles predicts superradiant states and a quantum yield that grows with network size, and steady-state spectroscopy finds the tryptophan quantum yield of microtubules (17.6 ± 2.1%) above that of free tubulin dimers (10.6 ± 0.6%). No lifetimes were measured, so the radiative rate itself was not, and the paper says nothing about consciousness, objective reduction or Orch OR. |
| [LIT-709](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-709.md) | Conceptualization of the Holobiont Paradigm as It Pertains to Corals | Goulet, Erill, Ascunce, Finley & Javan (2020), Frontiers in Physiology 11:566968, a review. A coral is a consortium: the animal plus the Symbiodiniaceae, bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses in its body, mucus and skeleton, and neighbours are excluded by definition. Membership can change, so one colony may be a different holobiont at different times. Traits such as thermal tolerance belong to the host–symbiont combination: not every Durusdinium is heat tolerant, and a novel anemone–alga pairing gave higher oxygen flux under heat than both natural ones. Measuring both partners shows different routes to the same bleaching outcome. Whether the holobiont is the unit of selection is asked, not answered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-555](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-555.md)); worth reading as a short, explicit statement of why a coral should be studied as a composite of host and microbes rather than as an animal with passengers. It is a mini-review with no data of its own (about 3,700 words), and its strongest point is conceptual: traits such as thermal tolerance belong to host–symbiont combinations, not to either partner. The physiological evidence it cites is thin and partly not from corals: its one demonstration that a combination is "not necessarily the sum of its parts" is an oxygen-flux experiment in the sea anemone Exaiptasia. It poses, and does not answer, whether the coral holobiont is a unit of selection. |
| [LIT-710](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-710.md) | Signaling cascades and the importance of moonlight in coral broadcast mass spawning | Kaniewska, Alon, Karako-Lampert, Hoegh-Guldberg & Levy (2015), eLife 4:e09991. Acropora millepora colonies from Heron Island, held in outdoor tanks for the eight days before the 2011 spawning night, spawned with the reef under ambient night light (21:30–22:30). They did not spawn that night under added light after sunset (N = 5) or under darkness (N = 5). 184 transcripts varied only on the spawning day, rose around gamete release in ambient colonies, did not change in dark ones and changed early in lit ones. Spawning-night genes were enriched for G-protein-coupled signalling; the proposed melanopsin and neuropeptide cascade is untested. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-557](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-557.md)); worth reading as the record's one experiment in which an environmental cue is manipulated and a collective biological timing event fails. Colonies of Acropora millepora held in outdoor tanks spawned with the reef only under natural night light. Colonies given artificial light after sunset, and colonies kept dark, did not spawn that night (N = 6, 5, 5). A second experiment found that blue, green and white nocturnal light delayed spawning by 6–8 h or 2 nights and red light did not. The signalling cascade (melanopsin-like opsins, neuropeptide G-protein-coupled receptors) is a model proposed from transcript changes and is not tested. The study shows each colony tracking a shared cue; it does not test coordination between colonies. |
| [LIT-711](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-711.md) | Phase Shifts, Herbivory, and the Resilience of Coral Reefs to Climate Change | Hughes et al. (2007), Current Biology 17(4):360–365. A replicated fish-exclusion experiment at Orpheus Island, Great Barrier Reef, begun in 2000 after the 1998 mass bleaching: four roofless 5 × 5 m cages, four partial cages and four open plots, over 30 months. Excluding large and medium fishes produced a phase shift to Sargassum-dominated macroalgae. Coral recovery was suppressed, through about two-thirds lower recruitment and more than double the mortality of surviving colonies. In the controls, coral cover nearly doubled to 20%, mainly by recruitment of taxa that bleaching had removed locally. Reopened cages lost their macroalgae within 30 days. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-558](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-558.md)), main text and methods; the supplement was out of reach. Worth reading as the controlled experiment behind the claim that reef recovery after bleaching depends on an ecological interaction, not only on surviving corals. On an inshore Great Barrier Reef crest after the 1998 bleaching, roofless cages kept large and medium fishes out of four 25 m² plots for 30 months. Macroalgae rose to a mean of 56% cover in the cages against 4.1% and 1.7% in partial cages and open plots. Coral cover in the cages rose only from 6.0% to 7.7%, against 19.2% and 20.2%, because recruitment was about two-thirds lower and mortality of established colonies more than double. It is one site with four replicates per treatment. The cages excluded all large and medium fishes, not herbivores alone, and the macroalgal state vanished within 30 days of reopening them. |
| [LIT-712](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-712.md) | Defining Coral Bleaching as a Microbial Dysbiosis within the Coral Holobiont | Boilard, Dubé, Gruet, Mercière, Hernandez-Agreda & Derome (2020), Microorganisms 8(11):1682, a review. Bleaching, the breakdown of the coral–dinoflagellate symbiosis, is redefined as a succession of three holobiont dysbiosis stages: (i) the microbiota buffers the stress and keeps essential functions; (ii) the algal partners are reorganised by shuffling or switching, with or without transient bleaching; (iii) the stress exceeds both buffers, symbionts are lost for good, opportunists invade and the coral dies, and at reef scale algae take over. The stages are a proposal, with no criteria to tell them apart, and the authors concede that microbial shifts are not shown to cause bleaching. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-556](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-556.md)); worth reading as the statement of the "adaptive dysbiosis" account of coral bleaching, which treats bleaching as three successive holobiont states: microbial buffering, reorganisation of the algal partners by shuffling or switching, and an irreversible breakdown ending in death. It is a review with no data of its own, and the account is a proposal. Its own text says that bacterial shifts during bleaching cannot yet be read as cause or consequence, so the title's "microbial dysbiosis" claims more than the body supports. |
| [LIT-740](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-740.md) | Cancer across the tree of life: cooperation and cheating in multicellularity | Aktipis et al. (2015), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 370:20140219. Multicellularity rests on five kinds of cellular cooperation, and cancer is cheating on them. Surveying cancer-like growth across the independent origins of complex multicellularity, the authors find division-of-labour cheating in every form, and resource and environment cheating so far only in animals and plants. Complex multicellularity is a cheater detection and suppression system. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-562](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-562.md)): in full, from the open-access deposit in PubMed Central (CC BY 4.0). Worth reading as a survey of cancer-like growth across the independent origins of multicellularity, read as cheating on five foundations of cooperation: proliferation inhibition, controlled cell death, division of labour, resource allocation and maintenance of the extracellular environment. Cheating on division of labour is reported in every form of multicellularity, and complex multicellularity is described as a cheater detection and suppression system. Limits: a literature review with no model or new data; absences may reflect lack of study, and animals' apparent susceptibility may reflect sampling. |
| [LIT-819](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-819.md) | Getting to the Bottom of Noether's Theorem | Baez (2020; chapter 2022), [ARXIV-2006.14741](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.14741). In Poisson algebras, complex *-algebras and Banach–Lie algebras, "a generates symmetries of b iff b generates symmetries of a" follows from the antisymmetry of the bracket and uniqueness of solutions; for a bilinear bracket, antisymmetry is the self-conservation principle {a, a} = 0. The nontrivial content is a map from observables to generators: in complex quantum mechanics multiplication by i, and in a unital JB-algebra Alfsen and Shultz's dynamical correspondence, whose second condition Baez links to "inverse temperature is imaginary time". | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-630](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-630.md)); worth reading as an account of what Noether's theorem, in its Hamiltonian form, actually assumes: given unique solutions of the flow equations, "a generates symmetries of b iff b generates symmetries of a" reduces to the antisymmetry of a bilinear bracket, which is equivalent to each observable conserving itself. The content lies in identifying observables with generators; in quantum theory that identification is multiplication by i, and Alfsen and Shultz's dynamical correspondence recovers it from a JB-algebra under the self-conservation principle and a second condition that Baez reads as "inverse temperature is imaginary time". The paper proves nothing new, by its own statement. |

(2026), bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.04.08.717352 (preprint, not peer reviewed). Reports that the PmrB sensor of the PmrA/PmrB two-component system in Acinetobacter baumannii detects sublethal oxidative stress via four periplasmic histidine residues coordinating a nickel cofactor; PmrA then activates iron-sulfur repair, a ferritin, a catalase and a peroxidase. The sensor is claimed to stay active 30--90 min after the stimulus is removed (a "response memory"), priming cross-protection against lethal peroxide and antimicrobial peptides, and the histidine box is reported necessary for virulence in mice and for hypervirulence in a clinical carbapenem-resistant isolate. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-656](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-656.md)) from the bioRxiv full-text PDF of the v1 preprint. An unrefereed preprint: worth keeping as a clean biological instance of the ``memory from a temporary signal'' pattern that THEORY-136 sets the evidential bar for, and as a self-contained worked example of a two-component signalling system (PmrA/PmrB) that is claimed to sense oxidative stress through a histidine box with a nickel cofactor, to hold a redox-gated conformational switch, and to retain a 30--90 minute ``response memory'' after the stimulus is removed. Read for what it shows, not for what a manuscript might use it for; its central memory and virulence claims rest on this single unreviewed study. |
| [LIT-853](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-853.md) | A heritable iron memory enables decision-making in Escherichia coli | Bhattacharyya, Bhattarai, Pfannenstiel, Wilkins, Singh and Harshey (2023), PNAS 120(48):e2309082120. In single-cell swarm assays (over 10,000 plates), an E. coli cell's swarming potential is shared by its fourth-generation descendants and lost by the seventh; it tracks the cell's iron status (low iron, better swarmer), iron starvation or forced uptake lengthens it, and a three-state switching model fits the lineages only with a fixed holding delay before switching. The state is not a bistable switch: an ODE of three swarming classes fits the lineage data only when each founding cell holds its class for a fixed delay (about three or four generations) before switching at constant rates. The "memory", "decision-making" and "conditioning" of the title and text are figurative; the iron link rests on a promoter reporter and on correlation, and the model fixes five parameters on two time points. |
| [LIT-854](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-854.md) | Irreversibility in bacterial regulatory networks | Zhao, Wytock, Reynolds and Motter (2024), Science Advances 10(35):eado3232. In Boolean models of the E. coli transcriptional regulatory network, a transient single-gene knockout or overexpression often moves the network to a different attractor, so one genotype can hold several heritable expression states without epigenetic marks. The genes able to do this are those upstream of, or inside, strongly connected components with positive circuits, and the more weighted paths to them the likelier. A prediction from a model ensemble, with no direct experiment. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-655](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-655.md)); worth reading as a whole-network test of whether transcriptional regulation alone can make a bacterium's state history-dependent.
