Model only: the paper runs no transient-perturbation experiment. Its one comparison with data, against strains evolved after a permanent crp knockout, mostly tests the sign structure of the network, and its link to irreversibility is weak (P = 0.03 on small counts). |
| [LIT-872](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-872.md) | Hyperbolic geometry of the olfactory space | Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018), Science Advances 4(8):eaaq1458. In four natural odour sources the rank order of correlations between compound concentrations has the clique-topology signature of points near the surface of a 3D hyperbolic ball and not of a uniform Euclidean cube, and human perceptual descriptions of 127 odorants have that of a full 3D hyperbolic ball. Pleasantness, boiling point and acidity read out as linear axes of the fitted fruit-odour space. The hierarchy that motivates the hyperbolic model is argued from biochemistry, not recovered from the data. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-672](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-672.md)); worth reading as the first application of clique topology to stimulus statistics rather than neural data, and as the Sharpee lab's first claim of a hyperbolic geometry in biology. For four natural odour sources (strawberry, tomato, blueberry, mouse urine; 45–78 compounds over 50–101 samples), the rank order of absolute concentration correlations gives Betti curves that match points sampled near the surface of a 3D hyperbolic ball (R_max = 7, R_min = 0.9 R_max, the same for all four) and reject uniform Euclidean cubes of any dimension tried. Human descriptor profiles for 127 odorants (Dravnieks) match a full 3D hyperbolic ball and no Euclidean cube. Linear axes for pleasantness, boiling point and acidity are found in the fitted fruit-odour space. The tree that motivates the hyperbolic model is argued, not recovered: compounds do not cluster by chemical class, and the only null geometry is a uniform Euclidean cube. |
| [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) v2 | Mutual information, neural networks and the renormalization group | Koch-Janusz and Ringel (2017; Nature Physics 14, 578–582, 2018). Defines the relevant degrees of freedom of a spatial block as the coarse variable that maximizes mutual information with the environment beyond a buffer, and learns it with restricted Boltzmann machines from Monte Carlo samples (the RSMI algorithm). It recovers Kadanoff block spins in the 2D Ising model and the electric-field variables of the dimer model, ignores decoupled noise, and, iterated, gives the Ising flow and ν ≈ 1.0 ± 0.15; a distribution-fitting RBM does none of this. The link to a short-ranged effective Hamiltonian is proved only in 1D. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-674](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-674.md)); worth reading as the paper that turns "the relevant degrees of freedom" of real-space renormalization into an objective that can be optimized: a block's coarse variable is chosen to maximize its mutual information with the system beyond a buffer around the block. Trained on Monte Carlo samples alone, the network rediscovers Kadanoff's block spin for the 2D Ising model, finds the low-momentum electric fields of the 2D dimer model while ignoring a strongly patterned but decoupled noise, and, iterated, reproduces the Ising flow away from T_c (located to about 1%) with ν ≈ 1.0 ± 0.15. An RBM trained instead to fit the data distribution latches on to the noise. The equivalence of the objective with a short-ranged effective Hamiltonian is argued, and shown only for 1D and quasi-1D chains; in 2D the evidence is the two models, whose answers were known beforehand. |
| [LIT-878](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-878.md) v2 | Statistical Physics through the Lens of Real-Space Mutual Information | Gökmen, Ringel, Huber and Koch-Janusz (2021; Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 240603). Replaces the RBM estimator of [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) with a neural InfoNCE lower bound co-trained with a convolutional coarse-graining filter (RSMI-NE), and uses the optimal filters at a single buffer size, not an iterated flow, as lattice forms of the most relevant operators. On the interacting dimer model they are the columnar and plaquette order parameters below T_BKT and the electric fields at high T; the maximal information marks the phases; one fitted scaling dimension (1.00037 against 1) is given. The optimality theorem is cited, not proved here. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-681](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-681.md)); worth reading as the paper that turns the real-space mutual-information principle of [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) from an iterated coarse-graining into a single-shot extraction of operators: with the mutual information estimated by a neural InfoNCE bound and the coarse-graining a convolutional filter trained against it, the filters that best compress what a block shares with its distant environment are, across the whole phase diagram of the interacting dimer model, the columnar and plaquette order parameters below the BKT transition and the electric fields at high temperature, and the plaquette filter's correlator gives a scaling dimension of 1.00037 against the predicted 1. The maximal information itself, log 4 in the ordered phase and decaying algebraically with the buffer in the critical one, traces the phase diagram. The theorem that the optimal filters are the most relevant operators is cited to another paper, and the model's operators were known beforehand. |
| [LIT-881](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-881.md) v2 | Optimal Renormalization Group Transformation from Information Theory | Lenggenhager, Gökmen, Ringel, Huber and Koch-Janusz (2018; Phys. Rev. X 10, 011037, 2020). Proves that a block coarse-graining keeping all the mutual information the block shares with the system beyond a buffer makes the coarse measure factorize across the block, so a finite-range Hamiltonian gains no range (1D; D dimensions under an extra assumption) and 1D disorder gains no correlations across it. For blocks of two spins of the 1D clean and dilute random Ising chain, where that condition is not met, couplings beyond nearest neighbour and disorder correlations shrink as more information is kept, vanishing at decimation. Encoding into a single binary spin explains why decimation wins in 1D and majority rule in a 2D toy model. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-682](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-682.md)); worth reading as the theory written for the RSMI algorithm of LIT-873: it proves that a coarse-graining which keeps all the information a block shares with the system beyond a buffer factorizes the coarse measure across that block, so a finite-range Hamiltonian does not gain range (in 1D; in D dimensions under an extra per-block assumption) and, for 1D disorder, no correlations are generated across the block. The full-capture condition is not met by the coarse-grainings it then studies: in its own 1D Ising example decimation keeps about half of the block's information, and the decay of next-nearest-neighbour and four-spin couplings, and of disorder correlations, as information grows is shown numerically for blocks of two spins. Its other result is information-theoretic: a single binary block spin loses information by encoding, which is why decimation beats majority rule in 1D and majority rule wins in a 2D toy model. |
| [LIT-882](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-882.md) | An exact mapping between the Variational Renormalization Group and Deep Learning | Mehta and Schwab (2014), arXiv preprint, never published in a journal. Identifies Kadanoff's variational RG kernel with an RBM's energy by T = −E + H, under which the coarse-grained Hamiltonian is the RBM's hidden-marginal Hamiltonian for any parameters and an exact RG step is a perfect fit of the data. Illustrates it with a hand-built decimation network for the 1D Ising chain and a four-layer stacked RBM trained on 2D Ising samples near T_c, whose receptive fields are local and grow with depth. It concedes that, short of exactness, RG and RBM training use different variational schemes; [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) shows the difference matters. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-683](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-683.md)); worth reading as the paper that first put deep restricted Boltzmann machines and Kadanoff's variational renormalization group side by side, and as the position Koch-Janusz and Ringel ([LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md)) argue against. Its "exact mapping" is an identification: setting the RG kernel T = −E + H makes the coarse-grained Hamiltonian equal the RBM's hidden-marginal Hamiltonian for every parameter value, and makes an exact RG step the same thing as a perfect fit of the data distribution. Away from that point the paper itself says the two procedures use different variational approximations, so the mapping does not show that training an RBM performs RG. The evidence that it does is a hand-built 1D decimation network and qualitative receptive fields of a stacked RBM on 2D Ising samples; no flow, fixed point or exponent is computed. |
| [LIT-885](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-885.md) | Relevance in the Renormalization Group and in Information Theory | Gordon, Banerjee, Koch-Janusz and Ringel (2020; Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 240601, 2021). On a cylinder, with block and environment as slabs separated by a buffer of length L_B, the information-bottleneck encoder just past its first transition depends on the block only through the boundary weak value of the leading transfer-matrix eigenvector, the lowest-dimension primary at large circumference, and the transition is at β_c = (λ0/λ1)^(2L_B). Checked on a three-site critical Ising cylinder. With a large enough alphabet the encoder respects the data's symmetry near that transition; a small one can break it. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-690](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-690.md)); worth reading as the theorem the real-space mutual-information programme ([LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md), [LIT-881](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-881.md), [LIT-878](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-878.md)) cites for its claim that the optimal coarse-graining picks out the most relevant operators. What it proves is narrower than that claim: for a short-range lattice model on a cylinder, with the block and the environment taken as whole slabs of the cylinder separated by a buffer, the information-bottleneck encoder just past its first transition depends on the block only through the boundary weak value of the leading transfer-matrix eigenvector, and the transition sits at β_c = (λ0/λ1)^(2L_B); for large circumference that eigenvector is the lowest-dimension primary. The planar block-in-a-shell geometry the algorithms use, the fixed-alphabet β → ∞ limit that is RSMI, and the regime beyond the first transition are not covered. A second result: past the first transition, with a large enough alphabet and no fine-tuning, the optimal encoder carries a representation of the data's symmetry, and a two-symbol example with Z4 symmetry breaks it. |
| [LIT-887](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-887.md) v2 | Why does deep and cheap learning work so well? | Lin, Tegmark and Rolnick (2016; Journal of Statistical Physics 168, 1223–1247, 2017). Argues that networks are cheap because physical data have low-order, local, symmetric Hamiltonians, and deep because data come from Markov generative hierarchies whose minimal sufficient statistics compose. Proves that a single hidden layer needs exactly 2^n neurons to multiply n inputs, against about 4n in a deep tree, and gives linear no-flattening examples. Holds that RG is supervised feature extraction, not unsupervised learning; arXiv v1–v2 carried a counterexample against [LIT-882](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-882.md) that hit a typo in its Eq. 8, and was dropped later. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-688](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-688.md)); worth reading as the third position in the dispute over whether deep learning performs renormalization, and for two results that stand on their own. On the dispute it holds that RG is "essentially a feature extractor for supervised learning": a coarse-graining is a renormalization only once the variables to keep are specified, and fitting the data distribution does not specify them. That holds, and it agrees with what [LIT-882](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-882.md) concedes and [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) shows; its sharper form was in an appendix of arXiv v1 and v2 only, dropped from v3 on and from the journal text, showing that a matched partition function does not give a matched distribution and (v2) that the exact trace condition is met by hidden variables that do not interact with the system at all. Its conclusion that RG has "little to do" with unsupervised learning is too strong: [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) gets the relevant variables without labels, from the far environment. On its own merits: a two-variable product needs four neurons and an n-variable product needs exactly 2^n in one hidden layer against about 4n in a deep tree (proved, in a Taylor-matching sense, with weights that grow without bound); the minimal sufficient statistics of a Markov generative hierarchy compose level by level (proved, and nearly immediate); that physics favours low-order, local, symmetric Hamiltonians, and that this is why cheap networks work, is argued, not shown. |
| [LIT-889](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-889.md) v2 | Symmetries and phase diagrams with real-space mutual information neural estimation | Gökmen, Ringel, Huber and Koch-Janusz (2021; Phys. Rev. E 104, 064106), the long companion of [LIT-878](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-878.md). Derives the RSMI-NE estimator in full and applies it to the 2D Ising model (1 bit below T_c, exponential decay with the buffer above it, boundary filters at T_c), the interacting dimer model and a 1D non-equilibrium chipping model. Its new object is the ensemble of optimal filters from independent runs: it maps an RSMI-degenerate subspace whose projections show broken and emergent (U(1)) symmetries, and PCA of it recovers the pristine operators. Every model's answer was known beforehand. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-692](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-692.md)); worth reading as the long companion of [LIT-878](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-878.md) and the place where the real-space mutual-information method is shown on more than one model and its outputs are read as an ensemble: the maximal information counts the ordered sectors (exactly 1 bit in the 2D Ising ferromagnet, 2 bits in the columnar dimer phase), decays exponentially with the buffer in the Ising paramagnet and algebraically at criticality, and the optimal Ising filter goes uniform, boundary and random across T_c; 500 independent runs per temperature map an RSMI-degenerate subspace of filters whose projections show the broken C4 and translation symmetries of the dimer model and, at high temperature, its emergent U(1), and PCA of the ensemble recovers the pristine operators from a window where they never appear alone. The number of coarse variables is chosen where the information stops growing. A non-equilibrium chipping model is a one-figure validation, and its formal status is said to be missing. |
| [LIT-891](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-891.md) | Comment on "Why does deep and cheap learning work so well?" | Schwab and Mehta (2016), arXiv comment, never published elsewhere. | [LIT-919](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-919.md) v2 | Nucleation | Vekilov (2010), Cryst. Growth Des. 10, 5007. For lysozyme, nucleation rates are about ten orders of magnitude below the classical prediction, and the paper places the error in the prefactor. The mechanism is inferred from a fitted model for one protein. | Active — read in full 2026-10-11 ([NOTE-708](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-708.md)), from the NIHPA author manuscript at PMC2995260; worth reading as the line's one clear statement, in a single paper, of classical nucleation theory (n* = 64Ω²α³/Δμ³, ΔG* = 32Ω²α³/Δμ²), of where it fails, and of the two things the author puts beside it: a solution–crystal spinodal, past which the nucleus is one molecule and there is no barrier, and the two-step mechanism, in which crystals nucleate inside metastable dense-liquid clusters that form fast, so that ordering inside them is the slow step. For metastable clusters the mechanism is inferred from a fitted kinetic model, not observed, and the claim that substrates act on the prefactor rather than the barrier is argued, not measured. | [LIT-920](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-920.md) v2 | Studien über die Bildung und Umwandlung fester Körper. 1. Abhandlung: Übersättigung und Überkaltung | Ostwald (1897), Z. Phys. Chem. 22, 289. Measures how small a seed can be (about 10⁻⁹–10⁻¹² g) and shows that only the solid itself or a strictly isomorphous solid seeds; separates metastable states (change only on contact with the new phase) from labile ones (spontaneous change); and states the rule later called the rule of stages: on leaving a state spontaneously, the form reached is the nearest in free energy, not the most stable. Offered as a frequent rule, not a law. | Active — read in full 2026-10-11 ([NOTE-709](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-709.md)), in German, from the public-domain scan of the volume at the Internet Archive; worth reading as the primary source of the rule later called the rule of stages, and of the metastable/labile distinction. Read §§26–41 (pp. 301–313): the definitions on p. 302, the rule on pp. 306–307 ("nicht der ... stabilste ..., sondern der nächstliegende"), and the conditional on p. 308 that a metastable intermediate stays until seeded unless it is labile with respect to the next form. Ostwald offers it "not as a law" but as "a frequently applicable rule" (p. 308), from a handful of cases and an analogy with the liquid–vapour isotherm, and absorbs exceptions by assuming unseen intermediates, a move he calls questionable (p. 309). Most of the paper measures seeds: only the solid or a strictly isomorphous solid seeds, down to about 10⁻⁹–10⁻¹² g. For du/dt = Au with A non-normal, the eigenvalues fix only the t → ∞ behaviour. Growth over time t is the top singular value of e^{At}, set at t → 0 by the numerical abscissa, the top eigenvalue of (A + A†)/2. Systems with every mode damped amplify perturbations by large factors before decaying, and their forced and white-noise responses exceed the equivalent normal response. Worked in a 2 × 2 example and damped Eady models. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-831](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-831.md)) in full; worth reading as the compact statement of non-modal stability for a fixed linear operator: growth over a finite time is the top singular value of the propagator, the eigenvalues govern only the long-run limit, and forced and stochastic responses exceed those of the normal system with the same spectrum. | [LIT-932](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-932.md) v2 | Hydrodynamic Stability Without Eigenvalues | Trefethen et al. (1993), Science 261, 578. Plane Couette and Poiseuille flow become turbulent at Reynolds numbers where eigenvalue analysis says they are stable. The proof modifies Isett's: a gluing step whose Reynolds stress stays trace-free, then Mikado-flow perturbations placed in disjoint "squiggling" space-time regions that cover every time, so energy can be pumped in even where the stress vanishes. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1013](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1013.md)) in full, from arXiv:1701.08678v1: worth reading for the admissible half of Onsager's negative direction: for every β < 1/3 and every smooth, strictly positive energy profile e(t) on [0, T] there is a weak solution of the 3D incompressible Euler equations on the periodic box, Hölder-continuous with exponent β in space and time, whose energy ∫\|v\|² equals e(t) at every time; taking e strictly decreasing gives solutions whose kinetic energy strictly decreases, so the energy flux into vanishing scales is one-signed on every time interval ([THEORY-776](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-776.md)); and for a shorter, more self-contained proof of the 1/3 threshold than Isett's ([LIT-1255](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1255.md)), with a trace-free glued stress and perturbations added everywhere in time so as to steer the energy. Read it knowing that "admissible" here means only that the total energy does not increase (the word appears in the title alone), not the local energy inequality, so the transfer is one-way for the whole box and may run backwards in places; that the same theorem gives solutions with increasing energy just as readily, so the direction is chosen by the prescribed profile and is not forced by the equations; that nothing is shown about vanishing-viscosity limits, about uniqueness or non-uniqueness for given initial data, or about the endpoint 1/3; that the h-principle (Theorem 1.3) rests on a result of Daneri and Székelyhidi stated without proof; and that the abstract's "typical" is looser than the weak-* density that Theorem 1.3 proves. |
| [LIT-1304](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1304.md) v2 | Discrete approach to stochastic parametrization and dimension reduction in nonlinear dynamics | Chorin & Lu (PNAS 2015). Proposes model reduction done entirely in discrete time: the resolved variables are advanced by a fixed numerical scheme plus a discrepancy sequence computed exactly from data, and the discrepancy is fitted as a NARMAX time series (autoregression in itself, lags of functions of the resolved variables, moving average in past innovations). Memory is thereby carried by finitely many lags. The connection to Mori–Zwanzig is drawn by analogy, not derived. On two-scale Lorenz 96 with ε = 0.5, a fit with one autoregressive lag, one or two exogenous lags and at most one moving-average term reproduces the statistics of x₁ better than a polynomial-plus-AR(1) closure, and at observation spacing 0.05 extends the lead time at anomaly correlation 0.6 from 2 to 4. | [LIT-1305](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1305.md) v2 | Nonuniqueness and existence of continuous, globally dissipative Euler flows | Isett (2017; Archive for Rational Mechanics and Analysis 2022). For every α < 1/15 there are weak solutions of the incompressible Euler equations on T³ (and T^d, d ≥ 3) in C^α_{t,x} that satisfy the local energy inequality ∂_t(\|v\|²/2) + ∇·((\|v\|²/2 + p)v) ≤ 0, strictly on an open time interval: the first continuous examples, and a first partial result on the strong Onsager conjecture. From one initial datum there is a Cantor family of them, with no isolated points, positive Hausdorff dimension in C_tL²_x and one common dissipation measure; the same holds for solutions with the local energy equality, and wild data are C⁰ dense. The scheme is a convex integration of "dissipative Euler–Reynolds flows" with one-directional transported plane waves, whose triad interactions cancel the unresolved energy flux current. In the proof the dissipation measure is a function of time alone, switched on only while the construction drains the solution to zero. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1027](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1027.md)), skimmed, from arXiv:1710.11186v4: the introduction, Sections 2 and 3 (the dissipative Euler–Reynolds flow and the Main Lemma), Sections 4.1–4.5 (the shape of the construction, the coefficient equations and the energy increment), the opening of 4.10, Section 4.14, Section 5 and Section 6 in full were read; Sections 4.6–4.13, the estimates, were paged through and not checked. Read it knowing that "globally dissipative" means the local energy inequality (not whole-box dissipation, and not strict); that the exponent 1/15 is far below 1/3 (De Lellis and Kwon later reached 1/7 in Hölder spaces, Giri, Kwon and Novack 1/3 in L³-based ones); that the dissipation happens only in a short final interval in which the construction drains the solution to zero, its timing an input; that the shared initial datum is produced by the construction, not prescribed; that the "probabilistic method" is a binary choice per stage, not a random construction; and that the Burgers example of §1.2.1 misstates two constants (−d/dt∫u₀² is 1/3, not 2/3, and the threshold (1/6)^{1/3} is sufficient but not sharp, which is (1/4)^{1/3}), without affecting its point. |
| [LIT-1307](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1307.md) v2 | Data-driven model reduction, Wiener projections, and the Koopman-Mori-Zwanzig formalism | Lin & Lu (J. Comput. Phys. 2021). Writes data-driven model reduction for an invertible map with an invariant measure in Koopman-operator terms, derives the discrete Mori–Zwanzig equation from the Dyson formula, and introduces the Wiener projection: orthogonal projection onto the span of the entire past of chosen functions Ψ of the resolved variables. Under it the memory term vanishes, the reduced equation is the causal Wiener filter x_{n+1} = Σ_k Ψ(x_{n−k})h_k + ξ_{n+1}, and the residual is orthogonal to all of Ψ's past. A rational approximation of the filter's transfer function, called "uncontrolled" by the authors, turns it into a NARMAX-type recursion. | [LIT-1670](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1670.md) v2 | Long-Range Order in a Two-Dimensional Dynamical XY Model: How Birds Fly Together | Toner & Tu (1995), PRL 75. A continuum theory of a flock: a coarse-grained velocity field with a convective term, a preferred speed and noise, coupled to a conserved density. Its linearized theory loses order in d ≤ 2, as the equilibrium XY model does under the Mermin–Wagner theorem, but the convective nonlinearity is relevant below d = 4, and in d = 2 symmetry gives z = 6/5, ζ = 3/5, χ = −1/5, so the velocity fluctuations stay bounded and the flock has true long-range orientational order. The exactness rests on a cubic vertex staying irrelevant, which the authors "strongly suspect"; the order also follows from z < 2, expected "on physical grounds". | Active — read in full 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1228](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1228.md)), from the arXiv preprint; worth reading as the founding hydrodynamic theory of flocking and as a clean case of order that an equilibrium system cannot have, stabilized by the coupling of order to transport. Its exponents are exact only on an argued-but-unproved step; its long-range order in two dimensions has a second, independent argument. |

A position paper by an 18-member network, two of whose authors led the Överkalix studies. It uses "transgenerational" for any outcome in offspring of an exposure in a parent before conception or in an earlier ancestor. In Överkalix cohorts of about 100 people each, a paternal grandfather's good food supply in mid-childhood went with higher mortality in his grandsons (rate ratio 1.67) and poor supply with lower (0.65); for paternal grandmothers and granddaughters, 2.13 and 0.72. They stay agnostic on mechanism and ask cohorts to collect ancestral exposure data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1320](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1320.md)), in place of [LIT-1764](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1764.md), which could not be fetched here; worth reading as the Överkalix authors' own later account of their findings and of how they answer the charges of multiple testing and cultural confounding. |
| [LIT-1708](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1708.md) | Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance: a critical perspective | Bird (2024). A Perspective by a DNA-methylation biologist. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance rests on two assumptions: that the environment instructs the epigenome, and that acquired marks reach the germline and affect offspring. Both are weak in mammals. Marks usually follow transcription factors rather than lead; DNA methylation is largely stripped from gametes and early embryos; no validated mechanism links environment to epigenome. Organisms work to erase marks (mice inherit them when Dppa2 is mutated). The Agouti diet effect did not replicate. The rodent effects are short-lived or unreplicated, and the one robust paternal effect (microbiome ablation) seems not to go through the sperm epigenome. The human claims are weak: the Swedish (Överkalix) study ignored cultural transmission, failed to replicate in a larger cohort, and risks multiple testing; the Holocaust FKBP5 study had 32 people. Human genetics keeps explaining conditions once put down to environment. The article does not separate inter- from transgenerational effects. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1264](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1264.md)) from the publisher's PDF (CC BY); worth reading as the most recent sceptical statement, and the only one of the three to name and dispute the human trauma claims. |

The authors call the evidence accumulating but preliminary: small samples, cross-sectional designs, unmeasured confounds, possible publication bias. They use "transgenerational" for any parent-to-child effect, in utero exposure included. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1310](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1310.md)), in place of [LIT-1692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1692.md), which could not be fetched here; worth reading as a brief, sympathetic account of the Holocaust FKBP5 study and the few human studies beside it, by authors not on that study (though Rutten has published with its second author, Daskalakis; ref. 13). |
| [LIT-1738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1738.md) | Molecular insights into transgenerational non-genetic inheritance of acquired behaviours | Bohacek & Mansuy (2015). Reviews rodent evidence that acquired behaviours and stress responses are transmitted through the germline, by sperm RNAs, DNA methylation and chromatin, and what remains open in humans. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher. The ETH Research Collection and the Zurich repository (ZORA) list it without a file, as they do Mansuy's other reviews of 2013–2017. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Jawaid and Mansuy 2019 ([LIT-1774](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1774.md)). |
| [LIT-1745](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1745.md) | Transgenerational Epigenetic Inheritance: Myths and Mechanisms | Heard & Martienssen (2014). A review of the mechanisms of epigenetic inheritance (small RNA, RNA-directed DNA methylation, paramutation, histone modification) and of germline reprogramming. Transgenerational inheritance is well documented in plants and nematodes, mostly at transposons and transgenes, and is rarely induced by the environment and more rarely adaptive. In mammals two rounds of reprogramming, in the germline and in the early embryo, erase most marks; the few bona fide epialleles (Agouti viable yellow, Axin fused) sit at retrotransposons. Effects of an exposed pregnant female count as transgenerational only from F3, of an exposed male only from F2. Human evidence, mostly nutritional (the Dutch famine, the thrifty phenotype), is intergenerational and confounded, so "so far there is little support"; human culture is the inheritance that is Lamarckian. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1254](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1254.md)) from the authors' accepted manuscript (PMC4020004), served by NCBI's PMC OAI-PMH service; worth reading as the standard map of epigenetic inheritance across plants, worms and mammals, and as the source of the F2/F3 rule the human trauma claims are measured against. |
| [LIT-1746](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1746.md) | Parental olfactory experience influences behavior and neural structure in subsequent generations | Dias & Ressler (2014). Male mice fear-conditioned to acetophenone or propanol before mating sired offspring (F1) and grand-offspring (F2) with heightened startle to, and lower detection thresholds for, the odour their F0 father was conditioned to, and not the other one. The offspring of acetophenone-trained males also had more M71 (Olfr151-expressing) olfactory neurons and larger M71 glomeruli; the anatomy, but not behaviour, was also tested and replicated in offspring conceived by IVF and carried by surrogates. Conditioning mothers before mating gave the same behavioural and anatomical effects, which survived cross-fostering. Olfr151 was less methylated in the sperm of conditioned F0 males (n = 12 vs 10) and of their naive F1 sons (n = 4 vs 4), but not in F1 or F2 olfactory epithelium. The authors read the effect as inherited sensitivity to a salient cue, not inherited fear, and leave open how an odour reaches sperm. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1281](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1281.md)) from the authors' accepted manuscript (PMC3923835), served by NCBI's PMC OAI-PMH service; worth reading as the standard animal case for germline transmission of a parent's experience: a specific, double-dissociated effect with IVF and cross-fostering controls, small groups, and a methylation result that is modest, confined to sperm and of unclear unit of analysis. This NOTE does not assess the later critique of the paper. |
| [LIT-1751](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1751.md) | Persistent epigenetic differences associated with prenatal exposure to famine in humans | Heijmans et al. (2008). Sixty people conceived during the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–45 had, about six decades later, less methylation in blood at the imprinted IGF2 gene's differentially methylated region than their unexposed same-sex siblings (0.488 vs 0.515, −5.2%, P = 5.9 × 10⁻⁵). Sixty-two people exposed only late in gestation, who were born lighter, showed no difference, and the timing interaction was significant. The authors read this as the first human evidence that a transient early-gestation exposure can be recorded as a lasting epigenetic change. The exposure is the person's own, in or around conception, so this is an intergenerational effect, not inheritance across untouched generations. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1248](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1248.md)) from the paper as reprinted in chapter 3 of Tobi's 2013 Leiden thesis (hdl.handle.net/1887/22065, Open Access); worth reading as the first human report of a prenatal exposure associated with a methylation difference decades later, and as the record's clearest case of the womb route: a mark from the person's own exposure, at the very start of gestation, with no claim about the next generation. |
| [LIT-1762](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1762.md) | A critical view on transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in humans | Horsthemke (2018). A Comment. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is documented in plants, nematodes and fruit flies; in mammals it must pass the Weismann barrier and two waves of reprogramming. Rodent reports mostly await independent confirmation, and the human ones (grandparental food supply, a Prader–Willi imprint) rest on unique cohorts. The Dutch Hunger Winter shows fetal programming, not germline transmission. Familial epimutations usually turn out to be secondary to a genetic variant. A proof needs: genetic, ecological and cultural inheritance excluded (F3 after an exposed pregnant female, F2 after an exposed male, with IVF and fostering); the factor found in pure germ cells; and the factor shown to cause the effect. In humans only genetic effects can be excluded. Cultural transmission very likely outweighs any epigenetic inheritance; the author remains sceptical. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1265](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1265.md)) from the published text (PMC6065375, CC BY), served by NCBI's PMC OAI-PMH service; worth reading as the shortest statement of what would prove germline epigenetic inheritance in humans, and of why the proof may be out of reach. |
| [LIT-1764](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1764.md) | Sex-specific, male-line transgenerational responses in humans | Pembrey et al. (2006). In historical records from Överkalix, Sweden, the food supply of paternal grandfathers in mid-childhood was associated with their grandsons' mortality, and that of paternal grandmothers with their granddaughters'. In the ALSPAC cohort, fathers who smoked early had sons with higher body mass. The authors propose sex-specific male-line transmission. | Unfetched — filed 2026-10-29, not read; set Unfetched the same day under [ADR-053](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-053.md): Nature marks the article free to read (nature.com/articles/5201538), but on 2026-10-29 the page served no body text and the PDF link redirected through Nature's sign-in back to the article page; it is not in PMC, and Unpaywall's submitted version is the abstract page. A human reader can likely open it. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unfetched until it is read, not on merit. Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Pembrey, Saffery and Bygren 2014 (LIT-1704). |
| [LIT-1774](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1774.md) | Inter- and transgenerational inheritance of behavioral phenotypes | Jawaid & Mansuy (2019). A short review from Mansuy's laboratory, the proponents' side. Rodent studies show that parental trauma, stress, drugs and in-utero insults pass behavioural phenotypes to offspring, in some models to the third or fourth generation, and that parental environmental enrichment passes benefits, and can prevent the transmission of trauma's effects. Germline dependence is shown by IVF and by injecting sperm RNA, which reproduces the phenotypes; non-coding RNAs are the best candidate carriers. Human studies of genocide survivors' descendants are offered as similar, and the review itself tables them as intergenerational. How a stimulus reaches the germline, and how effects pass beyond the first generation, are unknown. Germline reprogramming and the sceptics' objections are not discussed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1296](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1296.md)), in place of [LIT-1738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1738.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the proponents' short statement of the rodent case for germline transmission of behaviour, read in place of Bohacek and Mansuy 2015 ([LIT-1738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1738.md)), and for what it does not answer. |
| [LIT-1851](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1851.md) | Nonequilibrium phase transitions in coordinated biological motion: critical fluctuations | Kelso, Scholz & Schöner (1986), Physics Letters A 118(6):279–284. In bimanual wrist and finger movement paced to rising frequency, the standard deviation of relative phase grows as the anti-phase pattern nears its switch to in-phase and peaks in the transition, while the in-phase pattern shows neither growth nor a switch: the critical fluctuations HKB's stochastic extension predicts. Critical slowing is predicted, backed only by "very preliminary" spectral evidence, and left to later experiments. | Active — read 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1433.md)) in full, from an offprint scan posted on Kelso's lab page at Florida Atlantic University (https://ccs.fau.edu/hbblab/pdfs/Kelso_1986_PhysLettersA.pdf), read from the page images; worth reading as the first quantified report of critical fluctuations in human coordination: the standard deviation of relative phase rises before the anti-phase to in-phase switch and peaks in it, in wrist and finger experiments, with no such rise when the same movement starts in-phase. Read it knowing that its figures average a few subjects or show one representative subject, that it gives no statistical test, and that critical slowing and hysteresis are not measured in it. |
| [LIT-1861](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1861.md) | Can populations be healthy? Perspectives from Georges Canguilhem and Geoffrey Rose | Giroux (2021), HPLS 43:111. Canguilhem held that health and disease apply only to individuals taken as organic totalities, because normativity, the capacity to institute new norms, is anchored in the organism; at the population level he preferred "hygiene" or "salubrity". Giroux argues that debates over units of selection and biological individuality loosen his link between individuality and organism, and that social epidemiology (Rose's causes of incidence, integral variables such as herd immunity and social capital, multilevel models) gives reasons for a concept of population health not reducible to individual health, while denying populations the ontological unity of an organism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1452](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1452.md)), from the published article in PubMed Central (PMC8527978; made available in the PMC Open Access Subset under Springer Nature's COVID-19 terms), fetched as XML through the Europe PMC REST API. Worth reading for two things. It argues, from social epidemiology (Rose's population causes, herd immunity, integral variables), that some health properties belong to populations and not to their members, against Canguilhem's restriction of health to the individual organism. And it quotes Canguilhem's definition of health as normativity in his own (translated) words: "the possibility of tolerating infractions of the habitual norm and instituting new norms in new situations" (The Normal and the Pathological, 1991, pp. 196–197). The Canguilhem it reports is at second hand. |
| [LIT-1873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1873.md) | Dynamics governs switching among patterns of coordination in biological movement | Kelso, Scholz & Schöner (1988), Physics Letters A 134(1):8–12. When people switch on cue between in-phase and anti-phase finger movement, the switch from in-phase to anti-phase takes about twice as long as the reverse (four subjects, each p < 0.0001), with a longer-tailed distribution. Adding to the stochastic HKB equation a term that pulls relative phase toward the intended pattern reproduces the asymmetry and the distributions' shapes: intention acts within the pattern dynamics, not over them. | Active — read 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1449](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1449.md)) in full, from the publisher's PDF posted on Kelso's lab page at Florida Atlantic University (https://ccs.fau.edu/hbblab/pdfs/1988_Kelso_Scholz_Schoner_Dynamics_governs_switching_among_pattern.pdf); worth reading as the experiment showing that an intended switch between bimanual patterns is shaped by their stability: switching from in-phase to anti-phase takes about twice as long as the reverse, with a longer tail, as the HKB dynamics with an added intentional term predicts. Read it knowing that it has four subjects, that the model's one new parameter was set to match the order of magnitude of the switching times, and that the critical slowing it mentions is cited from an earlier paper, not shown. |
| [LIT-1885](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1885.md) v2 | Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation for Biomolecular Processes | Barato & Seifert (2015). In a nonequilibrium steady state of a Markov jump network obeying local detailed balance, the entropy produced while a current is counted times the current's squared relative uncertainty is at least 2k_BT, independent of time. Proved within linear response for any network and for unicyclic networks at any affinity, where the sharper bound is (A/N) coth(A/2N), which also tightens the Fano-factor bound on the number of states in an enzyme cycle. For multicyclic networks far from equilibrium it is a conjecture supported by numerics on seven networks. | Active — read in full 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1480](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1480.md)); worth reading as the letter that named the thermodynamic uncertainty relation: a current counted in a steady state with relative uncertainty ε costs at least 2k_BT/ε² of dissipation, proved within linear response and for single-cycle networks, conjectured with numerical support for many-cycle ones ([THEORY-1268](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1268.md)). It bounds the precision of currents, not of occupations. |
| [LIT-1890](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1890.md) v2 | Stochastic dynamics and non-equilibrium thermodynamics of a bistable chemical system: the Schlögl model revisited | Vellela & Qian (2009). The Schlögl model A + 2X ⇌ 3X, B ⇌ X by rate equation, chemical master equation and open-system thermodynamics. Bistability requires the two chemostats out of equilibrium. The master equation has one two-peaked stationary distribution, so the long-run occupancy of the two states is set by parameters and volume, not by the initial condition, and which state dominates can change with volume alone. The slow eigenvalue, exponentially small in volume, is the sum of the two escape rates. The more stable state can carry the higher or the lower entropy production, and the Fokker–Planck approximation can pick the wrong dominant state. | Active — read in full 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1474](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1474.md)) from the PMC copy; worth reading as the clearest worked case of a maintained chemical state that is metastable at finite size: bistability needs the chemostats out of equilibrium, long-run occupancy does not depend on the starting state, the slow eigenvalue is the sum of the escape rates ([THEORY-1273](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1273.md)), and entropy production does not pick the stable state ([THEORY-1270](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1270.md)). Its large-volume rate formula carries a spurious 1/V, so its reported breakdown of asymptotics is mostly that factor. |
| [LIT-1892](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1892.md) v2 | Macroscopic stochastic thermodynamics | Falasco & Esposito (2025). Takes stochastic thermodynamics of jump processes with local detailed balance to a large-size limit. Extensive rates and potentials give a deterministic dynamics whose Lyapunov function is the quasi-potential, and a large-deviation theory of fluctuations that keeps the fluctuation theorem. Equilibrium, linear irreversible and Onsager–Machlup theories are recovered as limits. Transition rates between attractors go as e^{−VΔI} and are bracketed by the entropy produced along relaxation and escape paths, tightly only near detailed balance. Each attractor has a housekeeping dissipation, and Langevin approximations miss it and misjudge barriers. Minimum and maximum entropy production principles hold only in special regimes. | Active — read in part 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1472](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1472.md), Skimmed: §§I–III, IV.A–D, IV.G–H, VI, VII.A.1, VIII and appendix A read in full; field theory and two of three applications not read); worth reading as the systematic statement of how maintained nonequilibrium states behave at large size: a quasi-potential, not a free energy, sets their lifetimes, which dissipation along relaxation and escape paths brackets ([THEORY-1264](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1264.md)); each carries its own housekeeping dissipation; and Gaussian-noise Langevin models get both barriers and entropy production wrong ([THEORY-1265](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1265.md)). |
